label: QUIET TOWN · A WEEK OF DECISIONS
deadline: Answer to the employer — on Sunday, by 12:00

ui.hubLead: Choose how to spend this slot. There isn’t time for everything.
ui.hubTip: There are more meetings in the week than slots: each one you live closes off another, and what you skip leaves a mark too.

intro.title: A week before the answer
paragraphs: On Monday a letter arrives: a job in another city. The answer is needed by Sunday noon. You have a week — eight time slots and five units of energy.
Talk to Mum, Dad, a friend, count the money or just go for a walk — there isn’t enough for everything. There’s no right ending here: every choice has its price.
intro.disclaimer: A fictional story. Choices in the game send nothing to your loved ones and don’t judge your real relationships.

clues.offer: The letter: a salary higher than your current one and a note, “start conditions can be discussed”. Answer by Sunday, 12:00.
clues.deadline: Answer to the employer — on Sunday, by 12:00. A delay is better asked for in advance.
clues.rent: Rita: rent in Ozyorsk is almost half the salary.
clues.lonely: Rita: the first three months there are lonely; a sports club and the neighbours on the stairs help.
clues.photo_sea: A photo by the sea: Dad looks younger and calmer in it.
clues.napkin: Nika’s napkin: on the left “what they expect”, on the right “what I want”. The right column is empty.
clues.dad_notebook: Dad’s notebook: expenses and addresses. Behind the worry — a wish to help.
clues.city_map: Rita sent a map: everything you need is ten minutes’ walk away.

scenes.title: A letter on the table
scenes.intro: On the kitchen table lies a letter: you’re offered a job in Ozyorsk. The answer is needed by Sunday, 12:00. Mum puts a cup in front of you and notices the envelope.

line.text: Are you really thinking of leaving? I’m used to you being here on Sundays.

objects.label: Letter
objects.text: A position, a salary higher than your current one and a note: “start conditions can be discussed”. Answer by Sunday, 12:00.

objects.label: Cup
objects.text: Mum remembers what tea you like. The care here is real — and so are the expectations.

choices.text: “I’m still thinking. It matters to me that you hear me out.”
choices.result: Mum looks into her cup for a long time. “I’m scared you’ll drift away. But go on — I’m listening.” For the first half-minute she really is quiet.
choices.trace: Mum heard the request to listen.

choices.text: “It’s my life. Don’t interfere.”
choices.result: Mum turns to the window. “Fine.” The boundary was stated, the conversation is closed. Behind the wall a door creaks — Dad heard.
choices.trace: The morning’s sharpness stayed between you.

choices.text: Put the letter in your pocket and change the subject.
choices.result: The letter ends up in your pocket. The talk about the weather goes smoothly — and strangely empty.
choices.trace: The letter is hidden. For now.

choices.text: Put the letter on the table and read it together with Mum.
choices.result: Mum reads the letter twice. “And housing? And who will you have there?” Her fear turns into a list of questions — that’s easier to work with than fear.
choices.trace: Mum read the letter herself.

choices.text: “Thanks for the tea. I need time — and for you not to rush me.”
choices.result: Mum smiles awkwardly. “I’m not rushing you. I’m just afraid of not having enough time.”
choices.trace: Mum heard the request for time.

scenes.title: The old backpack
intro: Evening. The backpack lies open on the bed — you’re checking the zips, having decided nothing yet. Dad knocks and, without asking about the city, first asks about the lock.

intro.text: He heard the morning conversation through the wall, so he moves more quietly than usual.
He adds: “Mum says you’re hiding something. I’m not asking what.”

line.text: If you decide to go — let’s at least check everything. I worry when you rush.

objects.label: Zip
objects.text: The zip sticks. Dad fixes it silently and with concentration — that’s his way of saying “I’m here”.

objects.label: A photo by the sea
objects.text: A photo by the sea: the three of you. Dad looks younger and calmer in it than usual.

choices.text: Ask Dad to help with a travel plan.
choices.result: He takes out a notebook. For the first time you discuss not “whether” but “how”.
choices.trace: Dad helps make a plan.

choices.text: Say you need time to think.
choices.result: Dad nods: “OK. Just don’t stay silent until Sunday — that’s harder than any answer.”
choices.trace: Dad gave you time but is waiting for words.

choices.text: Say there won’t be any move.
choices.result: Dad smiles with relief and closes the backpack. You feel uneasy: the words came before the decision.
choices.trace: Dad heard: “I’m not going anywhere.”

choices.text: Ask Dad how he once left home himself.
choices.result: “With one suitcase,” he laughs. “Grandpa didn’t speak to me for a week. For a long time afterwards I was afraid of doing the same to you — staying silent.”
choices.trace: Dad told you about his suitcase.

scenes.title: Talking to Nika
scenes.intro: Nika invites you to lunch. There are two napkins on the table: on one she draws a house, on the other a road.

cases.text: You seem more together. Has something become clear — or are you just pretending?
Listen, you have the face of someone hiding a cat. Spill it. And then: what do you want — not Mum, not Dad, not me?

objects.label: Napkin
objects.text: Nika drew two columns: “what they expect” and “what I want”. The right one is still empty.

objects.label: Nika’s phone
objects.text: Nika scrolls through photos: “Rita from our old team has been in Ozyorsk for two years. Call her — she’ll tell you what it’s really like.”

choices.text: Tell her what genuinely excites you about the offer.
choices.result: Nika slides over a clean napkin: “Write it down. Let your wish be on the table too.” You write three words — and are surprised by what they are.
choices.trace: The wish was said out loud.

choices.text: Admit you’re afraid of upsetting Mum.
choices.result: “Fear of upsetting someone is about love, not weakness,” says Nika. “But if you decide only because of it, later you’ll resent everyone.”
choices.trace: Nika heard the fear.

choices.text: Ask not to discuss it for now.
choices.result: Nika puts the napkins away and tells a story about a neighbour and a parrot. You laugh for the first time in three days. The topic hasn’t gone anywhere, though.
choices.trace: A breather without the conversation.

choices.text: Fill in the right column of the napkin completely.
choices.result: Six lines come out. Two surprise you, one scares you. Nika folds the napkin neatly: “Keep it.”
choices.trace: The napkin of wishes stayed with you.

scenes.title: Calling Rita
scenes.teaser: Rita from the old team lives in Ozyorsk.
scenes.intro: Rita picks up on the second ring. You can hear a tram — it’s evening in Ozyorsk.

line.text: Oh, it’s you. Nika wrote that you’re thinking about moving. Ask anything — no sugar coating.

objects.label: Map
objects.text: Rita sends a map: her home, the office, the park. Ten minutes’ walk to everything — that’s true.

objects.label: Rita’s notes
objects.text: Rita has a list of first-month mistakes. Item three: “didn’t calculate the cost of living”.

choices.text: Ask how much it really costs to live there.
choices.result: Rita names the figures: rent is almost half the salary, a studio near the metro costs more. “But without this number you can’t decide honestly.”
choices.trace: Real figures appeared.

choices.text: Ask what the first months there are like.
choices.result: “Lonely. For three months, almost every evening. Then a climbing club and the neighbour on my stairs.” She doesn’t try to convince you.
choices.trace: Rita told you about the loneliness.

choices.text: Ask directly: “Is it worth going?”
choices.result: Rita laughs: “I’ll tell you how it was for me. The choice is yours.” There’s no answer, but a hint appears about what else to ask.
choices.trace: The decision stayed with you.

choices.text: Ask her to send the list of first-month mistakes.
choices.result: A minute later the list arrives. You read it twice: half the mistakes can be predicted in advance.
choices.trace: You have a list of someone else’s mistakes.

cases.text: There’s something to clarify in the note.
The letter is unanswered.
The letter is open on the screen. The note about “start conditions” is right there — now you need to decide what to do with it.
The offer letter sits in your inbox. You read it on the run — the details slip away. The cursor blinks in an empty reply field.

objects.label: Calendar
objects.text: Until Sunday, 12:00 — four days. A delay is possible, but it’s better to ask for it in advance.

objects.label: The note
objects.text: At the end of the letter: “start conditions and the format of the first weeks are negotiable”.

choices.text: Clarify the start date, the format of the first weeks and the answer deadline.
choices.result: An hour later the answer comes: the first three weeks can be remote, the start date is moved by a month. The answer deadline stays the same.
choices.trace: A remote start is agreed.

choices.text: Ask for an extra week to think.
choices.result: “We can wait until next Friday,” the recruiter writes. A delay isn’t a gift but an agreement, and now it’s on record.
choices.trace: The delay is agreed.

choices.text: Reply with a general “thanks, I’m thinking it over”.
choices.result: The letter goes. Nothing has changed — but at least the question of whether you replied at all isn’t hanging.
choices.trace: A polite reply was sent.

scenes.title: A call from Mum

cases.text: Mum learned about the backpack from Dad.
Mum calls after the morning conversation.
Mum called twice.

scenes.intro: The phone screen says “Mum”. Outside it’s a quiet evening. You can answer now or text that you’ll call later.

cases.text: Dad said you’re packing a backpack. Why do I hear about this from him?
It hurt this morning. But I don’t want us to stop talking.
I thought about our conversation. I’m still worried, but I want to understand your plan.
You rarely tell me what’s going on with you. I worry.

objects.label: Phone
objects.text: Two missed calls. Mum doesn’t call for no reason — she usually texts first.

objects.label: Geraniums
objects.text: Mum’s geraniums on the balcony: she repots them every spring. A minute of quiet brings your breath back.

choices.text: Tell it as it is: there’s no decision, you’re gathering information.

cases.text: Mum is silent, then: “Thank you for telling me. Even if not right away.” There’s hurt in her voice — and relief.
Mum asks a lot of questions, but now you decide which of them to answer.

choices.trace: Mum knows there’s no decision yet.

choices.text: Text: “I’ll call tomorrow, right now I want to rest.”
choices.result: Mum replies with a short “OK”. The conversation is postponed, the connection remains.
choices.trace: The conversation with Mum is postponed.

choices.text: Don’t answer.
choices.result: Silence helps for the evening. But the missed calls pile up — Mum will surely tell Dad about them.
choices.trace: The call went unanswered.

choices.text: Ask: “Were you scared back then?”
choices.result: A pause. “Every day,” says Mum. “I just didn’t tell anyone.” You hear her talk about herself for the first time, not about you.
choices.trace: Mum told you about her fear.

scenes.title: The market with Mum
scenes.teaser: Mum asked for help with the shopping. No big talks.
scenes.intro: Mum has long asked you to go to the market with her. No talk about the city — just being together: bags, the queue, tomatoes.

line.text: Take this basket. And don’t look at the prices, I’ve written everything down.

objects.label: List
objects.text: The list is in Mum’s handwriting; it has things you love. The care here is literal.

objects.label: Stall
objects.text: The seller asks whether you’re home for long. Mum silently rearranges the apples.

choices.text: Just help and don’t raise the topic.
choices.result: You carry the bags and laugh at the prices. Mum seems to breathe out. The conversation is postponed, but the warmth stays.
choices.trace: A day with Mum without talking about the city.

choices.text: On the way, say: “Let’s talk about the letter after the market.”
choices.result: Mum nods: “OK. After the market.” She answers more briefly than usual but doesn’t walk away.
choices.trace: Agreed to talk after the market.

choices.text: Keep looking at your phone the whole time.
choices.result: Mum notices and says nothing. You return home each lost in your own thoughts.
choices.trace: The day was spent side by side, but not together.

choices.text: Ask about the old album: “Shall we get it out tonight?”
choices.result: Mum freezes for a second. “It’s on the top shelf. Let’s get it.”
choices.trace: Mum agreed to get the album out.

scenes.title: The old album
scenes.teaser: The album from the top shelf.
scenes.intro: Evening. The album smells of dust and glue. Mum turns the pages as if looking for one in particular.

line.text: Here. I’m twenty-two. I left home with one suitcase.

objects.label: Photo
objects.text: Young Mum at the station, with a suitcase and a defiant look. Behind her is a woman who isn’t smiling.

objects.label: Caption
objects.text: On the back: “Left. Mum didn’t see me off.”

choices.text: Say: “You were scared back then. And now too.”
choices.result: Mum looks at the photo for a long time. “I’m scared now too,” she says. “Only now it’s for you.”
choices.trace: Mum told you the story of her leaving.

choices.text: Ask what she would have wanted to hear back then — from her own mum.
choices.result: “That I would manage. That I wasn’t betraying anyone,” Mum answers. “Well, now I know what to tell you.” She smiles through tears.
choices.trace: Mum realised what she wants to tell you.

choices.text: Listen without saying anything.
choices.result: She talks for a long time: about the station, about her first rented room. You remember not the words but how her voice changes.
choices.trace: Mum’s story was heard to the end.

choices.text: Joke: “So I take after you.”
choices.result: Mum laughs, but a little stiffly. The moment closed before it could open.
choices.trace: A joke replaced the conversation.

scenes.title: Family dinner
scenes.teaser: Dad invites you to dinner: “Let’s discuss money and housing.”
scenes.intro: You come to dinner. Dad sets out the plates and carefully starts talking about money, housing and the new job.

cases.text: I looked up the route. If needed, I’ll help with the move. Do you already know what you want?
You said you’re not going anywhere. It seemed to me that’s not the whole truth.
I remembered my suitcase. If you decide to go — just say it properly, not through the wall.
I’m not sure it will all work out there. How will you cope?

objects.label: Keys
objects.text: The keys to your parents’ house are in your pocket. You can keep them in any city.

objects.label: Dad’s notebook
objects.text: Dad wrote down expenses and addresses — neatly, as always. Behind the worry — a wish to help.

choices.text: Discuss the practical questions without handing the decision to Dad.

cases.text: You come with figures, and for the first time that evening Dad doesn’t interrupt. “That’s… reasonable,” he admits.
You argue about the budget, then find two useful points. Dad feels heard.

choices.trace: The practical questions were discussed.

choices.text: Ask to talk about something else tonight.
choices.result: Dad puts the notebook away. Dinner goes on; you can come back to the plan later — but later keeps getting shorter.
choices.trace: The talk about the plan was postponed.

choices.text: Agree with every worry and give up your plans.
choices.result: Dad relaxes. And something tightens inside you: your words agreed, but you didn’t.
choices.trace: All of Dad’s worries were accepted without objection.

choices.text: Take the notebook and check the budget together.
choices.result: You lean over the page as if over a map. Dad finds a mistake in the calculations and for the first time is glad to be listened to.
choices.trace: The budget was checked with Dad.

choices.text: Say: “You talked about the suitcase. I need you to believe in me, not to play it safe for me.”
choices.result: Dad is silent. Then: “Grandpa didn’t say that to me back then. I’ll try.” He wipes his hands on a towel, though they’re dry.
choices.trace: Dad heard the request to believe in you.

scenes.title: Night calculations
scenes.teaser: A spreadsheet that needs filling in.
scenes.intro: Late evening. The laptop glows. The spreadsheet is still empty: the salary in one cell, the unknown in all the others.

cases.text: The salary is higher than now, but rent is almost half. Add travel and a first month without a cushion, and it’s tight.
The salary is higher than now. The other cells are empty — there’s too much you don’t know yet (it would be good to ask someone who lives there).

choices.text: Calculate honestly, with a margin for the unexpected.

cases.text: By the middle of the night the spreadsheet comes together. It’s tight, but with a margin for the first two months. Anxiety becomes a number — you can work with that.
The spreadsheet takes shape, but half the rows are guesses. You mark them yellow: these are questions for people who live there.

choices.trace: The budget was calculated honestly.

choices.text: Count only the pluses — for inspiration.
choices.result: The numbers shine. You close the laptop feeling light, but at the edge of your mind a question remains: what about the minuses?
choices.trace: The budget was calculated with pluses only.

choices.text: Close the laptop and go to sleep.
choices.result: The calculations can wait. Sleep is part of the decision too, and tonight it matters more than the spreadsheet.
choices.trace: Sleep turned out more important than the spreadsheet.

scenes.title: A walk without the phone
scenes.teaser: Go out without a route. Energy will return.
scenes.intro: You leave your phone at home and go out without a route. You know the street down to its cracks, but today walking feels different.

objects.label: Signpost
objects.text: One arrow points to the station, the other to the river. Neither marks the right way.

choices.text: To the river.
choices.result: By the water, thoughts slow down. The question “what do I want” doesn’t sound scary — just like a question.
choices.trace: A walk by the river.

choices.text: To the station.
choices.result: The timetable on the board. Ozyorsk is four hours away. That’s not infinity. A one-way ticket and a return ticket differ by one word.
choices.trace: Now you know the train timetable.

choices.text: Past the school and the old courtyard.
choices.result: The courtyard seems smaller than you remember — which means life has grown wider over the years.
choices.trace: A walk through the old courtyard.

scenes.title: Nika writes
scenes.teaser: Nika hasn’t heard from you for several days.
scenes.intro: Your phone: “Are you OK? For three days I’ve only heard about you from your mum.” Nika isn’t blaming you — she’s just writing.

line.text: You don’t have to answer in detail. But answer something.

objects.label: Messages
objects.text: Nika sent three — each shorter than the last. The last one: “Just say you’re there.”

choices.text: Call right now.
choices.result: Nika answers on the first ring: “Finally.” Ten minutes later you’re laughing, and twenty minutes after that she mentions Rita from the old team: “Call her, she’s in Ozyorsk.”
choices.trace: Back in touch with Nika.

choices.text: Text: “Everything’s fine, just a lot going on. I’ll tell you.”
choices.result: Nika sends a smiley and “waiting”. The bridge is built, but nobody has crossed it yet.
choices.trace: A short message was sent to Nika.

choices.text: Don’t answer.
choices.result: The screen goes dark. The silence feels like rest — until you remember there’s a person on the other end too.
choices.trace: Nika got no answer.

final.title: Your own route
final.subtitle: the answer is needed by 12:00
intro: Sunday, 11:20. The station, platform two. Forty minutes until noon.

cases.text: Mum stands by a pillar with a thermos — she came, though she didn’t promise to.
Mum isn’t on the platform. On your phone: “Call me later.”
Dad checks the lock on the backpack for the hundredth time.
Dad sent a message: “Whatever you decide — tell me straight.”

intro.text: Nika waves from the other side of the platform with a paper cup.

lines.text: I was scared back then too. Tell me what you decide — and I’ll try to listen to the end.
I’ll still miss you. But tell me what you’re deciding for yourself.
I don’t understand why change a familiar life. But I want to hear your answer.

options.text: Go and see Ozyorsk and come back with a decision.

cases.text: You already know the timetable — and you buy a return ticket for Saturday. It’s not a contract, it’s reconnaissance.
You get a return ticket for Saturday. It’s not a contract, it’s reconnaissance.
Accept the offer with a remote start.
Accept the offer and start preparing the move.

lock.reason: There isn’t enough clarity yet: talk, calculate or take a walk — and come back to this choice another time.

options.result: You send your acceptance. Your hands tremble slightly, but inside there’s the quiet after words finally said out loud.

options.text: Stay and take up your own project.

lock.reason: Staying can truly be your own decision when you know what you want: talk to Nika, fill in the napkin, take a walk.

options.result: You write “thank you, no” and immediately open the notes on your own project. It’s not giving up on life, but a decision in its favour.

lock.reason: A delay needed to be agreed in advance. On Sunday it’s already too late.

options.result: The deadline is Friday next week. Time doesn’t run away from a decision if you use it.

cases.text: A new address, the same connection
Stay and choose your own
Time that was used well
A road you can think along

A month has passed. The trip to Ozyorsk gave you facts: streets, flats, prices, people. There’s no decision yet — but the questions have become more precise. Mum sends a photo of the cat: “How’s the city?”
A month has passed. For the first three weeks you work remotely from your room and pack, and then you move to Ozyorsk. Mum sends a photo of the cat: “We miss you, but keep telling us.”
A month has passed. You live in Ozyorsk: the boxes are half unpacked, the neighbours in the building nod hello. Mum sends a photo of the cat.
A month has passed. You stay in your city and work on your own project. On Sundays you and Mum still see each other — only now it’s a choice, not a habit.
A month has passed. The delay gave you time to visit Ozyorsk, talk to people who live there and reach an answer without rushing. The answer has been sent — you know which one and why.
Talks with Mum have become longer and calmer. She still sighs into the phone, but now she asks: “And how are you?” — and waits for the answer.
It has become easier to talk about plans with Mum, even when you disagree.
Things with Mum are even: you call on Sundays, she’s still getting used to it.
Things with Mum are still tense. You write briefly. But the door to a conversation isn’t closed — either of you can take the next step.

paragraphs.text: She still remembers the missed call that week.

cases.text: Dad sent a spreadsheet of expenses and a list of repairmen — his way of being there. And for the first time he wrote: “I believe in you.”
Dad sent a spreadsheet of expenses and a list of repairmen — that’s his way of being there.
Dad remembers the words “I’m not going anywhere” and carefully asks what changed. That’s a conversation still to come.
Things with Dad are calm: worry more often turns into practical help.
It’s still hard for Dad not to decide for you. Specific agreements help.
Nika framed the napkin with the right column — “so you don’t forget what you want”.
You and Nika are in touch: she’s still the first to ask how you really are.
You and Nika are in touch, though less often than you’d like.
You and Nika have barely talked since that week. The phone lies nearby, and the first step hasn’t been taken yet.
The first month turns out more expensive than in the spreadsheet. Not a disaster, but now it’s clear why people calculate with a margin.
The expenses fit: the margin you set aside that night came in handy.
You understand well what you wanted from this week, and it shows in the little things.
Some questions became clearer, some remained. That’s a normal result for one week.
Sometimes you come back to the question of what you really want. The answer doesn’t have to come within a week.
